kept: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator: liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct, and the universe of six substances is uncreated. It can accept 'one truth, many names' only in its own way — as many-sidedness (anekānta) about a plural reality — not as the identity of all souls in one substance.
other: Jainism denies a single ultimate being: the liberated are infinitely many individual souls, alike in nature but not one. In Jain terms 'all is one' is the collective standpoint (saṃgraha-naya), true of things only in respect of their common character 'existence', and false when made absolute (the Jain reading of Vedāntic monism). A reading of 'ekaṃ sat' as one reality would be accepted only in that limited standpoint; Haribhadra's 'one goal, many names' concerns the one state of liberation, not one soul.

kept: Can liberating knowledge be combined with ritual action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya), or does knowledge alone liberate?
other: Does liberation require knowledge combined with ritual works, or knowledge alone (or devotion)?

kept: Are there objects external to cognition?
How does a sentence convey its meaning: by the connection of word-meanings already expressed (abhihitānvaya) or by words that express meanings already connected (anvitābhidhāna)?
other: How does a sentence convey its meaning?

kept: Is the root impurity (āṇava mala) a real substance removable only by ritual initiation, or is it ignorance - a contraction of consciousness - removed by knowledge?
other: Is the root impurity (āṇava mala) a real substance removable only by ritual initiation, or is it ignorance removed by knowledge?

kept: How many means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) are there?
other: How many means of knowledge are valid?

kept: What is the status of the Veda: authorless and eternal (apauruṣeya), breathed out or composed by the omniscient Lord, or without authority?
other: The status of the Veda: authorless, God-authored, or rejected?

kept: Is there a self (ātman, puruṣa, jīva) — an enduring conscious subject distinct from body and changing cognitions — or only a stream of impersonal factors designated 'person'?
Is there an Īśvara — a Lord who makes the world and dispenses the fruits of action? Is he proved by reason, known only from scripture, a special puruṣa for meditation, or not to be accepted at all?
other: Is Īśvara real, needed, or a special puruṣa?
Does the omniscient (kevalin) take food and undergo hunger and the other hardships?

kept: Can Mahāmudrā be introduced and realized apart from tantric empowerment — Gampopa's 'sūtra Mahāmudrā', the 'white self-sufficient remedy' — or is Mahāmudrā only the wisdom arising from empowerment and the two stages?
other: Is there a Mahāmudrā outside tantric empowerment (sūtra or 'white panacea' Mahāmudrā)?

kept: Should a Mādhyamika establish emptiness by autonomous inferences (svatantra-anumāna) or only by consequences (prasaṅga) that draw out untenable consequences of the opponent's own thesis — and does this difference of method reflect a difference of view?

Is the ultimate empty of its own nature like all phenomena (rang stong, self-emptiness), or empty only of what is other than it — the adventitious stains — while not empty of its own nature and qualities (gzhan stong, other-emptiness)?
other: Empty of self, or empty of other?

kept: Personal affiliation of Naiyāyikas with the Pāśupatas and a shared account of the means of knowledge.
other: Religious affiliation of several Naiyāyikas (and Vaiśeṣikas) with Śaiva / Pāśupata traditions

kept: Principles of scriptural interpretation, the authority of the authorless Veda, and the view of the two Mīmāṃsās as one science.
other: The view that Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā are one śāstra, and a theistic reading of Jaimini (Vedānta Deśika's Seśvaramīmāṃsā and Mīmāṃsāpādukā).

kept: Śaiva ascetic institutions, maṭhas and sites in Karnataka that passed from Kālāmukha to Vīraśaiva hands
other: Temples and monasteries in Karnataka (and possibly members) passing from Kālāmukha to Vīraśaiva hands.

kept: The epistemological framework and vocabulary of Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's school - the particular and the conceptual, exclusion (apoha/apohana), self-awareness, causal efficacy - taken up by Utpaladeva and turned against the no-self thesis.
other: Utpaladeva states the Buddhist logicians' position (momentary cognitions, no enduring knower, apoha, self-awareness) as the pūrvapakṣa of the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā and turns its tools (ābhāsa, self-awareness, the refutation of external objects) toward a single conscious Lord.

kept: Abhinavagupta's aesthetics - rasa as the relishing (carvaṇā) of consciousness, śānta as a rasa - drawing on his Śaiva doctrine.
other: Abhinavagupta's reading of rasa as the relish of consciousness at rest in itself (camatkāra, viśrānti) and of śānta's stable basis as the self.

kept: Nāth initiation and yoga through Gahinīnāth to Nivṛtti and Jñāneśvar
other: Initiation lineage (Gahinīnāth → Nivṛttināth → Jñāneśvar) and the kuṇḍalinī yoga of Jñāneśvarī 6

kept: The vocabulary and imagery of sahaj, śūnya, anahad nād, gagan maṇḍal, the tenth door and ulaṭbāṃsī used by Kabīr and other Sants
other: Yogic vocabulary and images: sahaj, śūnya/sunn, the unstruck sound, the tenth door, the sky-circle with dripping nectar, iḍā–piṅgalā–suṣumnā, unmanī, the 'avadhū' address, upside-down speech

kept: Gorakṣa (Korakkar) and Matsyendra (Macchamuni) among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars
other: Identification of Maccamuṉi and Kōrakkar with Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha; the goal of the perfected, deathless body; the title 'nātar' for the masters

kept: Nāth siddhas counted as rasa-siddhas and rasa authors (Carpaṭi, Nityanātha); the ideal of an immortal, perfected body shared.
other: The goal of the perfected, deathless body and siddhas who are also alchemists (Nityanātha, Carpaṭi, Nāgārjuna in some lists)

kept: The three humours (vātam, pittam, kapam), the seven tissues and much Sanskrit medical vocabulary shared by Āyurveda and Siddha medicine.
other: The humoral triad, seven body-constituents, six tastes and rejuvenation (rasāyana/kaṟpam)

kept: The Kaula ritual and doctrinal frame: kula conduct, the secret use of the five 'M's, the eight bonds (pāśa), the four seats (Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna), yoginī hierarchies and the āmnāya scheme.
other: The Kaula mode of Śrīvidyā worship and the Dakṣiṇāmnāya placement of Tripurasundarī

kept: The name of Rām as the saving Name; the claim of initiation of Kabīr, Ravidās, Pīpā, Sen and Dhannā by Rāmānanda
other: Rāmānanda counted guru of Kabīr, Raidās, Pīpā, Sena and Dhanna; the Rām-nām

kept: Nāmdev's Hindi padas and his example as a low-caste devotee saved by the Name
other: Nāmdev's Hindi songs and example revered by Kabīr and later northern Sants

kept: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and its three-doṣa medicine, translated into Tibetan (in the Tengyur); scholars trace much of the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi) to it.
other: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya's medicine — the eight branches, the three doṣas with five subtypes each, the seven constituents and three wastes, the six tastes and potencies, daily and seasonal regimen, rejuvenation and virility — which reappears, with Buddhist causation and other additions, in the Four Tantras.
8th–12th c. (translations; compilation of the Four Tantras)

kept: The framework of Buddhist logic — inference for oneself and for others, fallacies of thesis and reason — adopted and argued against in Jain logic (Nyāyāvatāra; Akalaṅka's replies to Dharmakīrti).
other: The two-means framework reinterpreted (pratyakṣa/parokṣa), the debate over the triple-marked reason (answered by 'anyathānupapatti' as the sole mark), and the genres of logic manuals.

kept: Mind-only as the account of conventional reality, adopted as the step before the emptiness of mind.
other: Mind-only accepted as the conventional truth and as a stage of meditation before the imageless (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla).

kept: The distinction of difficult and easy paths; the reading of birth as 'birth of non-birth' from Tanluan's Sanlun training.
other: The 'easy practice' of calling to mind the Buddhas' names in the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā ascribed to Nāgārjuna; Nāgārjuna as the first of Shinran's seven patriarchs.

kept: Recitation of the name within Chan monasteries; dual cultivation; Chan masters as Pure Land patriarchs (Yanshou, Zongze, Tianru).
other: Recitation of Amitābha's name within Chan (Jingzhong assemblies, Yanshou, Zhuhong, Ōbaku).
